problems.statement: About 1100 B.C., Chinese astronomers measured the maximum height of the Sun on the days of summer and winter solstices. In the former case, they obtained the value $h_1=79^\circ07'$, in the latter case $h_2=31^\circ19'$. On both the occasions, the Sun was south of zenith. Find out at what latitude the observations were made. Also calculate the angle between the ecliptic and the celestial equator in the epoch mentioned.

solution.statement:
The latitude may be found by formula:

$$\varphi=90^\circ-\frac{h_1+h_2}{2}=34^\circ47'.$$

The angle between the ecliptic and the celestial equator in the epoch mentioned:

$$\varepsilon=\frac{h_1-h_2}{2}=23^\circ54'.$$

problems.statement: The “Iridium” satellites give brilliant flares due to reflection of sunlight from their highly polished main mission antennas which are highly reflective plates, each of size $188\times86$ cm. A satellite was overhead at the time of the flare and the apparent magnitude of the flare was $-8^m$ at the centre.

solution.statement:
The drawing enables to realise that the light from the satellite actually spreads in a cone with angle $\alpha=0.5^\circ$, so that it covers area on the ground

$$S_E=\pi(\alpha h/2)^2.$$

Using the relation $m_1-m_2=-2.5\log(b_1/b_2)$ and taking into account stellar magnitude of the Sun $m_1=-26.8^m$ and magnitude of the flare $m_2=-8^m$, we can find that $(b_1/b_2)\approx3.3\cdot10^7$, and so we see $1/(3.3\cdot10^7)$ part of the Sun through the reflecting plate.

It means that the visible projection of the square of the plate $188\times86$ cm ($S=1.62$ m²) is $1/(3.3\cdot10^7)$ part of $\pi(\alpha h/2)^2$. Projection gives some factor about $2^{1/2}$ which should be taken into account since as usual we see the plate under the angle of $45^\circ$ (see figure):

$$S=\frac{2^{1/2}\pi(\alpha h/2)^2}{3.3\cdot10^7}.$$

Taking into account that $\alpha=9.1\cdot10^{-3}$ rad, one can find that $h\approx750$ km and the area on ground covered by the beams from one antenna

$$S_E=\pi(\alpha h/2)^2\approx40\ \mathrm{km}^2.$$

parts.label: a)
parts.statement: Draw a ray diagram and make a rough estimate of the area on ground covered by the beams from any one of the antennas.

parts.label: b)
parts.statement: Find the height of the satellite above the surface of the earth.

problems.statement:
We have received a message from Extraterrestrial Intelligence. Please decode it. The message is:

`10001100010011001001001001100111100100110010010010011001001000110`

(This is the whole message, not part of it.)

solution.statement:
There are 65 signs in the message. Having presented it as the table $5\times13$ (the alternative versions are not possible), we receive two possible solutions:

**5 columns, 13 lines**

```text
10001
10001
00110
01001
00100
11001
11100
10011
00100
10010
01100
10010
00110
```

**13 columns, 5 lines**

```text
1000110001001
1001001001001
1001111001001
1001001001001
1001001000110
```

After replacement of units on signs, and zero on gaps, the second version yields the quite understandable message:

![](p3-message)

“International Astronomical Union” or “1 astronomical unit”.

figures.alt: Original dot-pattern message: IAU or 1 AU.

problems.statement: Imagine that you are a polar bear, sitting on North Pole through the year 2002. Calculate, how large part of the sky (in %) is below the ecliptic at the moment when the sun was or will be at its highest position above the horizon. At what moment (to within a day) the same part of the sky will appear under the ecliptic once again? To explain the solution draw a picture with a polar bear on North Pole.

solution.statement:
Not only for the moment when the sun was or will be at its highest position above the horizon but in every moment the part of the sky below the ecliptic is equal to $\varepsilon/\pi$ is below than line of ecliptic.

$\varepsilon$ is the angle between the ecliptic and the celestial equator ($23^\circ26'$ in 2002) and $\pi=180^\circ$. So the answer is $23^\circ26'/180^\circ\approx0.13$. Answer: 13 %, at any moment.

problems.statement:
In the attached table you will find the following data about the comet C/2002 O4 (Hoenig): orbital elements and ephemeris (date, right ascension, declination, distance to Earth, distance to Sun, elongation, phase and stellar magnitude). Calculate the speed of the comet at perihelion using the given data. Note: the orbital speed of Earth is $V_E=30$ km/s.

![](p5-ephemeris)

solution.statement:
One can find from the first part of the table that the eccentricity of the orbit is $e=1.000812$. It is very near to a parabolic orbit. I.e. speed of the comet in perihelion is about $2^{1/2}$ of the circular speed with the same distance from Sun.

Than one can find from the ephemeris that the distance Sun–Comet in perihelion is $a_c=0.776$ a.u. (02.10.2002.). Using the III Kepler law ($T^2/a^3=\mathrm{const}$) one can find that for the circular speed

$V^2a=\mathrm{const}$

and so:

$V\sim a^{-1/2}.$

I.e.

$$V_c=V_E(a_c/a_E)^{-1/2}=V_E(0.776)^{-1/2},$$

where $V_E\approx30$ km/s is the circular speed of Earth.

$$V_p=2^{1/2}V_E(a_c/a_E)^{-1/2}=V_E(2a_E/a_c)^{1/2}=V_E(0.388)^{-1/2}\approx48\ \mathrm{km/s}.$$

figures.alt: Complete original bilingual comet ephemeris and orbital-elements table.

problems.statement: An elevator operates between Earth’s surface and a geostationary satellite. Estimate (at least roughly), at what distance below the satellite will the effective gravity be equal to one hundredth of the usual value.

solution.statement:
Finally necessary to find the distance $x$ where $g_{\mathrm{eff}}=0.01g_0$.

$$g_{\mathrm{eff}}=GM/R^2-\omega^2R=g_0R_0^2/R^2-\omega^2R,$$

where $g_0$ and $R_0$ are values near the earth surface. But at first necessary to find the radius $R_S$ of the geostationary satellite's orbit; at this position $g_{\mathrm{eff}}=0$:

$$GM/R_S^2=\omega^2R_S,$$

$$R_S^3=GM/\omega^2=g_0R_0^2/\omega^2=g_0(R_0T/2\pi)^2,$$

where $T$ is period of the Earth revolution.

$$R_S=\{g_0R_0^2/\omega^2\}^{1/3}\approx42\,200\ \mathrm{km}.$$

For small variations one may use formula

$$g_{\mathrm{eff}}(A+x)=g_{\mathrm{eff}}(A)+g_{\mathrm{eff}}'x.$$

So in measuring gravitation very near the satellite (the satellite is zero point and $g_{\mathrm{eff}}=0$), for the small variations of the distance $x$ directed from Earth,

$$g_{\mathrm{eff}}(x)=g_{\mathrm{eff}}'x=(-2GM/R_S^3-\omega^2)x.$$

So for $g_{\mathrm{eff}}=0.01g_0$ one can calculate

$$x=\frac{0.01g_0}{-2GM/R_S^3-\omega^2}=\frac{0.01g_0}{-2g_0R_0^2/R_S^3-(2\pi/T)^2}.$$

Taking into account that $R_S^3=g_0(R_0T/2\pi)^2$,

$$x=\frac{0.01g_0}{-3(2\pi/T)^2}\approx-6150\ \mathrm{km}.$$

The sign 'minus' means that these 6150 km are in a direction opposite to our axis direction: the position of the point before the satellite. Of course, the value 6150 km already is not a 'small variation', but it is enough to make desirable estimation: about **6000 km**.
